title: Prime-to-characteristic level rigidity for polarized abelian varieties
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field], [def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A/k$ be an abelian variety [def-sc-abelian-variety], and let $\lambda:A\to A^\vee$ be a polarization. A polarization of an abelian variety $A$ over an algebraically closed field means a homomorphism $\lambda:A\to A^\vee$ induced by an ample [def-sc-ample] invertible sheaf [def-sc-invertible-module] $L$, namely $x\mapsto[t_x^*L\otimes L^{-1}]$, where $t_x$ is translation by $x$ and $A^\vee=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{A/k}$ is the dual abelian variety representing algebraically trivial invertible sheaves, rigidified at the identity. A polarization is principal when $\lambda$ is an isomorphism. For a group automorphism $a$ of $A$ (an automorphism of the $k$-group scheme $A$ [def-sc-group-scheme]), its dual $a^\vee$ is pullback on $A^\vee$; preserving $\lambda$ means $a^\vee\lambda a=\lambda$. Let $n\geq3$ be an integer invertible in $k$, let $[n]:A\to A$ be multiplication by $n$ [def-sc-mult-n], and write $A[n](k)=\{x\in A(k):[n]x=0\}$. If a $k$-group automorphism $a:A\xrightarrow{\sim}A$ preserves $\lambda$ and satisfies $a(x)=x$ for every $x\in A[n](k)$, then $a=\mathrm{id}_A$.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 14.4(b), printed p.62; polarization convention in I §11, printed p.51. We retain the prime-to-characteristic hypothesis needed when testing geometric torsion points.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-polarized-abelian-automorphisms-finite], the group $G=\operatorname{Aut}_k(A,\lambda)$ is finite. The given $a$ belongs to $G$. Among $1,a,a^2,\ldots,a^{|G|}$ two powers $a^i,a^j$ with $i<j$ agree; cancellation gives $a^r=\mathrm{id}_A$ for $r=j-i\geq1$.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 14.4(b), printed p.62, using 14.4(a), 10.15, 8.12 and 14.5.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-abelian-hom-finite-free] with $B=A$, the $k$-group endomorphisms of $A$ form a ring $R=\operatorname{End}_k(A)$ under pointwise addition and composition, with $1_R=\mathrm{id}_A$, and its additive group has a finite $\mathbf Z$-basis. The difference $f=a-1_R$ is therefore a $k$-group homomorphism. For every $x\in A[n](k)$ the hypothesis gives $f(x)=a(x)-x=0$.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 14.4(b), printed p.62, using 14.4(a), 10.15, 8.12 and 14.5.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-abelian-torsion-kernel-divisibility] to $f:A\to A$ and this same $n$. Its hypotheses hold because $k$ is algebraically closed, $n\geq3$ implies $n\geq1$, $n$ is invertible in $k$, and step 2 verified vanishing on every $n$-torsion point. Obtain $b\in R$ with $f=b\circ[n]_A=n b$. Thus $a=1_R+n b$.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 14.4(b), printed p.62, using 14.4(a), 10.15, 8.12 and 14.5.

proof.text: The ring $R$ of step 2 has a finite $\mathbf Z$-basis, step 1 gives $a^r=1_R$ with $r\geq1$, and step 3 gives $a=1_R+n b$ with $n\geq3$. Applying [lem-sfb-finite-free-ring-congruence-torsion] to these objects yields $a=1_R$. Since $1_R=\mathrm{id}_A$ as a group-scheme morphism, this is the asserted equality $a=\mathrm{id}_A$.
